hypotheses.text: The null sets the parameter equal to a benchmark. The alternative specifies greater than, less than, or different from that benchmark.
hypotheses.title: Three research questions

errors.text: Alpha is the false-rejection probability under the null. At a specified alternative theta, beta is the probability of not rejecting, and power is one minus beta.
errors.title: Two errors, different conditions

power.text: For a right-sided known-SD mean test, reject above benchmark plus critical z times SE. Power at a specific alternative mean is one minus the normal CDF at critical z minus the standardized effect.
power.title: Power for a right-sided z test

tails.text: For a symmetric standard normal or t reference distribution with CDF G: right tail uses q above the 1-alpha quantile and p=1-G(q); left tail uses q below the alpha quantile and p=G(q); two tails use absolute q and twice the upper tail.
tails.title: One rulebook for symmetric z and t tests

z.text: For independent normal observations and known population variance, the mean has variance sigma squared over n. Under the null the standardized mean is exactly standard normal.
z.title: Known population variance: z test

t.text: The sample variance divides squared residuals by n minus one. Under independent normal sampling and the null, substituting sample SD gives a t statistic with n minus one degrees of freedom.
t.title: Unknown population variance: t test

t-proof.tex: Z=\frac{\overline X-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\sim N(0,1),\quad U=\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1},\quad Z\perp U,\quad T=\frac Z{\sqrt{U/(n-1)}}
t-proof.text: Under the normal null model the standardized mean is normal, the scaled sample variance is chi-square, and these are independent. Their ratio defines Student t.
t-proof.title: Why estimating SD changes the reference distribution

wald.text: For IID data with positive finite variance, the CLT plus consistency of sample SD gives an asymptotically normal studentized mean by Slutsky’s theorem.
wald.title: Large-sample Wald justification

ci.text: Not rejecting a two-sided test is equivalent to the null value lying between the matching confidence limits, up to the stated boundary convention, when the statistic uses the same standard error.
ci.title: Invert a test to obtain an interval

onebound.text: A one-sided lower confidence bound is mean minus the 1-alpha critical value times SE; an upper bound is mean plus that margin.
onebound.title: Matching one-sided confidence bounds

proportion.text: With independent Bernoulli trials, successes are binomial. Test the null probability using its own binomial variance in the denominator and a large-sample normal approximation.
proportion.title: One proportion: null-based standard error

prop-proof.text: A sample proportion is the average of independent binary indicators. Its mean is pi and its variance is pi times one minus pi divided by n.
prop-proof.title: A proportion is a mean of zeros and ones

groups.tex: \overline X_j=\frac1{n_j}\sum_iX_{ji},\quad S_j^2=\frac{\sum_i(X_{ji}-\overline X_j)^2}{n_j-1},\quad E(\overline X_j)=\mu_j,\quad E(S_j^2)=\sigma_j^2
groups.text: For each group j, define its own sample mean and unbiased sample variance. Their expectations are the corresponding population mean and variance.
groups.title: Keep group summaries separate

difference.text: Independent normal samples give a normally distributed difference of sample means. Its variance is the sum of the two mean variances.
difference.title: Independent differences add variances

pooled.text: Pool the within-group residual sums of squares, weighting the group variances by their degrees of freedom and dividing by total degrees of freedom.
pooled.title: A pooled estimate of one common variance

pooled-test.text: Under independent normal sampling, equal population variances, and null mean difference delta zero, the pooled t statistic has n1 plus n2 minus two degrees of freedom.
pooled-test.title: Pooled two-sample t test

pooled-ci.text: The pooled confidence interval is the observed mean difference plus or minus the t critical value times the pooled standard error.
pooled-ci.title: Confidence interval for the mean difference

pooled-proof.text: With a common population SD sigma, standardize the mean difference by sigma times the square root of the sum of reciprocal sample sizes. The pooled scaled variance is independent chi-square, giving the t ratio.
pooled-proof.title: Derive the pooled t distribution

welch.text: Welch’s statistic divides the mean difference minus the null difference by the unpooled standard error. Its approximate t degrees of freedom are the squared sum of variance contributions divided by the sum of squared contributions over their group degrees of freedom.
welch.title: Welch–Satterthwaite approximation

welch-ci.text: Welch’s approximate confidence interval uses the unpooled standard error and its fractional degrees of freedom.
welch-ci.title: Welch confidence interval

welch-proof.text: Under normal samples the estimated variance V has mean A and variance twice the sum of squared true variance contributions divided by group degrees of freedom.
welch-proof.title: Moment matching behind Welch’s degrees of freedom

welch-match.text: Match V to a scaled chi-square with the same mean and variance; equating variances gives the effective degrees of freedom. Replace population variances by sample variances in practice.
welch-match.title: Approximate the variance estimate, then form a t ratio

paired.tex: D_i=X_{1i}-X_{2i},\quad\overline D=\overline X_1-\overline X_2,\quad S_D^2=\frac{\sum_i(D_i-\overline D)^2}{n-1},\quad T=\frac{\overline D-\Delta_0}{S_D/\sqrt n}\overset{H_0}{\sim}t_{n-1}
paired.text: For n matched pairs compute one difference per pair, its mean and sample variance. A one-sample t test on independent normal differences has n minus one degrees of freedom.
paired.title: Paired data become one sample of differences

paired-ci.text: The paired confidence interval uses the SD of differences. Difference variance equals the two variances minus twice their covariance.
paired-ci.title: Pairing retains within-unit covariance

twoprop.tex: \widehat p_j=\frac{k_j}{n_j},\quad\widehat p_{\rm pool}=\frac{k_1+k_2}{n_1+n_2},\quad Z=\frac{\widehat p_1-\widehat p_2}{\sqrt{\widehat p_{\rm pool}(1-\widehat p_{\rm pool})(1/n_1+1/n_2)}}\overset{H_0}{\approx}N(0,1)
twoprop.text: Under the null of equal population proportions, estimate the common probability by total successes over total trials. Standardize the observed difference using the pooled null standard error.
twoprop.title: Compare two independent conversion rates

twoprop-var.text: Independent proportion estimates add variances. Under equal population proportions, the population variance simplifies to a common pi factor.
twoprop-var.title: Why the null permits pooling

twoprop-ci.tex: (\widehat p_1-\widehat p_2)\ \pm\ z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\widehat p_1(1-\widehat p_1)}{n_1}+\frac{\widehat p_2(1-\widehat p_2)}{n_2}}
twoprop-ci.text: The basic large-sample confidence interval for a proportion difference uses separate observed proportions in an unpooled standard error.
twoprop-ci.title: Unpooled Wald interval for the difference

f-test.text: For independent normal populations, the sample variance ratio divided by its hypothesized population ratio has an F distribution. Equal variances uses r0 equal to one.
f-test.title: The variance-ratio F test

f-tails.tex: \begin{array}{c|c|c}H_1&\text{Rejection rule}&p\text{-value}\\r>r_0&f\ge Q_F(1-\alpha)&1-G_F(f)\\r<r_0&f\le Q_F(\alpha)&G_F(f)\\r\ne r_0&f\le Q_F(\alpha/2)\ \text{or}\ f\ge Q_F(1-\alpha/2)&\min\{1,2\min[G_F(f),1-G_F(f)]\}\end{array}
f-tails.text: F tests use their nonsymmetric CDF and quantile function: right and left tail probabilities for one-sided tests; twice the smaller tail, capped at one, for the equal-tail two-sided test.
f-tails.title: F tails are not symmetric

f-proof.text: Scaled sample variances from independent normal samples are independent chi-square variables. The ratio of each divided by its degrees of freedom defines the F distribution.
f-proof.title: Derive F from two chi-square variables

f-reciprocal.text: Taking an F reciprocal swaps numerator and denominator degrees of freedom. A p quantile is the reciprocal of the one-minus-p quantile with swapped degrees of freedom.
f-reciprocal.title: Swapping groups swaps the degrees of freedom

f-ci.text: A confidence interval for the population variance ratio divides the sample variance ratio by the upper and lower F quantiles in reverse order.
f-ci.title: Confidence interval for a variance ratio

depth-pooled-variance.text: The pooled variance is 49 times 16 plus 39 times 9, divided by 88, about 12.8977 square minutes.
depth-pooled-variance.title: Pool residual sums, not standard deviations

depth-pooled-test.text: The pooled SE is the square root of 1135 over 88 times the sum of 1 over 50 and 1 over 40, about 0.7618 minutes. The difference of minus 2 minutes divided by this SE gives t about minus 2.6252.
depth-pooled-test.title: Convert pooled spread to the uncertainty of a difference

depth-welch-se.text: A contributes 0.320 square minutes and B contributes 0.225 square minutes. Welch SE is the square root of their sum, about 0.7382 minutes.
depth-welch-se.title: Add separate sources of uncertainty

depth-welch-df.text: Welch effective degrees of freedom are 0.545 squared divided by 0.320 squared over 49 plus 0.225 squared over 39, about 87.6730.
depth-welch-df.title: Retain the fractional reference degrees of freedom

depth-prop-pool.text: The pooled proportion is 58 successes over 90 visitors, equivalently a sample-size-weighted mean of 0.60 and 0.70, about 0.64444.
depth-prop-pool.title: Pool visitors rather than averaging percentages

depth-prop-test.text: The null SE uses pooled success and failure probabilities and reciprocal sample sizes. It is about 0.10154. Dividing minus 0.10 by it gives z about minus 0.9848.
depth-prop-test.title: Compute surprise under the equal-rate model

depth-prop-interval.text: The unpooled interval SE is about 0.10025. The 95 percent interval is minus 0.10 plus or minus the 0.975 standard normal quantile times that SE, about minus 0.29649 to 0.09649.
depth-prop-interval.title: Estimate a difference without imposing equality

depth-f-reciprocal.text: The upper-tail probability above 1.5 with 49 and 39 degrees of freedom equals the lower-tail probability below two thirds with 39 and 49 degrees of freedom, about 0.09637.
depth-f-reciprocal.title: A reciprocal changes which tail holds the same evidence
